- Agave hearts (piñas) are cooked, by steaming in ovens or roasting in pits, which turns inulin into sugar before crushing.
- Potatoes are cooked until they break down, then treated with bought-in enzymes.

### Stage 2: fermentation
Fermentation turns sugar into alcohol. Yeast feed on the sugar and produce ethanol, carbon dioxide (which escapes) and many minor compounds called congeners. One important group, the esters, smells fruity. Fermentation usually stops at about 8-10% abv.
This stage matters more than many candidates expect. Distillation can only select and concentrate what is already in the liquid: a congener that was not created in fermentation cannot appear in the spirit. That is why most distillers use carefully chosen yeast, and why some rum makers deliberately push fermentation to build intense tropical fruit aromas.

### Stage 3: how distillation works
Distillation separates parts of a liquid by boiling and condensing. Ethanol boils at about 78°C and water at 100°C. When an alcoholic liquid boils, the vapour is therefore richer in alcohol than the liquid it came from. Collect that vapour, cool it in a condenser, and you have a stronger liquid.
Distillation does two jobs at once. It concentrates ethanol, and it selects congeners, keeping some and leaving others behind. The strength at which the spirit is collected decides how much flavour survives.
Distillation strength | Aroma intensity | Typical examples
Below 80% abv | Medium to pronounced | Cognac, malt whisky, Bourbon, Tequila, heavy rums
Around 90% abv | Light | Light rum marks, Scottish grain whisky
95-96% abv | Neutral | Neutral spirit used for vodka, gin and liqueurs
The rule to remember: the higher the distillation strength, the lighter the spirit. Neutral spirit is defined by law as at least 95% abv in the USA and at least 96% abv in the EU.

### The pot still: parts and double distillation
A pot still is a batch still. It is filled, run, emptied and cleaned, and then the cycle starts again. Most are made of copper, which is easy to shape and conducts heat well. Learn the parts in the order the vapour travels:
- Heat source: usually steam coils or a steam jacket; Cognac stills must be heated by direct flame.
- Pot: holds the liquid to be distilled; a drain empties it afterwards.
- Still head and neck: the vapour rises here; the height and shape influence the style.
- Lyne arm (Scotland) or swan neck (Cognac): the pipe that carries vapour to the condenser.
- Condenser: cold water turns vapour back into liquid, either in a shell and tube design or a traditional worm tub (required in Cognac).
One pass through a pot still is not enough to make a spirit, so most pot still spirits are distilled twice.
The first distillation mainly removes water. The fermented liquid, at about 10% abv, is boiled and the distiller collects everything until the flow is almost pure water. The result, called low wines, is only about 25-30% abv, because a lot of water comes over with the alcohol. The watery residue is discarded.
The second distillation selects flavour. The low wines go back into a still together with the heads and tails from the previous run, and the distiller makes two cuts:
- Heads: the first few minutes of liquid, rich in very volatile compounds that smell of solvent. These are set aside.
- Hearts: when the solvent smell fades, the flow is switched to the spirit receiver. This is the part that will be sold, usually about 70-75% abv overall.
- Tails: after some hours, heavier compounds with cheesy or plastic notes appear. The flow is switched back and collected until it is almost water.
Heads and tails are recycled into the next batch, so no good alcohol or flavour is wasted. Because a pot still separates compounds only roughly, many congeners travel with the hearts. That gives pot still spirits a medium to pronounced aroma intensity.

### The column still: plates and continuous distillation
A column still is a tall vertical still divided by horizontal plates. Every plate acts as a small still, so many distillations happen at once, one stacked on top of another. As long as the flow in equals the flow out, the column can run continuously.
- Heat source: steam, usually through a heat exchanger, sometimes injected directly into the base.
- Plates: each holds a layer of boiling liquid; the plates near the top have the highest strength.
- Bubble caps: force rising vapour to bubble through the liquid on each plate.
- Downcomers: carry overflowing liquid down to the plate below.
Hot fermented liquid enters near the base, vapour rises, and liquid falls. The most volatile compounds reach the top and are drawn off as heads. Heavier ones gather lower down and are taken off as tails. Watery waste leaves from the base. The hearts can be drawn from whichever plate gives the strength the distiller wants. A short column with few plates gives a flavourful, low-strength spirit, as in Armagnac or rhum agricole. A tall column with many plates can reach 95-96% abv.

### Pot still vs column still compared
 | Pot still | Column still
Operation | Batch: one run, then empty and clean | Continuous while in balance
Distillations needed | Usually two (sometimes three) | Many at once, on each plate
Maximum strength | Well below 90% abv | Up to 95-96% abv
Separation of flavours | Rough: many congeners kept | Precise: chosen by the plate
Typical spirit | Medium to pronounced intensity | Neutral to pronounced, depending on height
Classic uses | Cognac, single malt Scotch, heavy rums, top Tequilas | Vodka, grain whisky, light rum, Bourbon, Armagnac
A common exam trap: column stills do not only make neutral spirits. Bourbon and Armagnac are mostly column-distilled, yet both are full of character because they are collected at low strength.

### Stage 4: what happens after distillation
Every new spirit is colourless and dry. Post-distillation decides the colour, aroma, sweetness and strength of the final product. The main operations, in their usual order, are maturation or storage, adding other flavours, blending and finishing.

### Oak vs inert vessels
Oak barrels change a spirit in four ways. They add colour, which moves from lemon to gold, amber and, in rare cases, brown. They add aromas such as vanilla, coconut, cinnamon and clove. Over time, oxygen slowly enters the barrel and creates more complex notes like leather, dried fruit and mushroom, often called rancio. Finally, evaporation of water and alcohol (the angels' share) concentrates what remains, while the charred or toasted inner surface removes some harshness.
Three choices shape how much the oak gives:
- Barrel age: a new barrel gives the most colour and flavour; each refill gives less.
- Previous contents: barrels that held Bourbon, Sherry or other wines release some of that liquid back into the spirit.
- Warehouse temperature: heat speeds up exchange with the wood, which is why spirits mature faster in a hot climate.
Inert vessels, usually stainless steel or glass, add no colour and no flavour. Most unaged spirits rest in them only briefly, so they stay close to the new spirit. Longer storage can make a spirit smoother and rounder while it stays colourless. Very old Cognacs are sometimes moved into glass demijohns to stop further change.

### Blending, colour, sugar and dilution
Blending has two aims: consistency from one batch to the next, and complexity that no single barrel or spirit could give alone. The wider the range of spirits a blender can use (pot and column, young and old, different casks), the easier both aims become.
Finishing prepares the spirit for the bottle:
- Colour: tiny amounts of caramel colour correct small differences between batches. Caramel adds colour, not sweetness.
- Sugar: any sweetness you taste was added after distillation. It is optional for some spirits and required for liqueurs.
- Filtration: chill-filtration stops haze when a spirit gets cold; activated charcoal can strip colour and flavour, as in some white rums and vodkas.
- Dilution: pure water brings the spirit down to bottling strength. Legal minimums are usually 37.5% abv in the EU and 40% abv in the USA.

### Common mistakes and study tips
- Confusing sweet aromas with sweetness: vanilla in a Bourbon is an aroma; the spirit is dry unless sugar was added.
- Thinking colour proves age: caramel can colour an unaged spirit, and charcoal can remove colour from an aged one.
- Mixing up strengths: about 10% after fermentation, 25-30% for low wines, about 70-75% for pot still hearts, 95-96% for neutral spirit.
- Forgetting that distillation cannot create flavour, it can only select what fermentation produced.
The best way to fix this topic is to draw both stills from memory, label each part and trace the vapour and liquid. Then explain the diagram aloud in two minutes. The Wine Goat app turns this into short lessons, flashcards and practice questions with explanations, so you can check yourself in a few minutes a day.
Q: What is the difference between a pot still and a column still?
A: A pot still works in batches: it is filled, run and emptied, and most spirits need two runs. It separates flavours roughly, so the spirit is lower in strength and richer in aroma. A column still runs continuously, with many distillations happening on its plates at the same time, and can reach 95-96% abv, the strength needed for neutral spirit.
Q: Why are most pot still spirits distilled twice?
A: One pot still run cannot lift a fermented liquid of about 10% abv to spirit strength. The first run removes water and gives low wines of about 25-30% abv. The second run concentrates the alcohol further and lets the distiller separate heads, hearts and tails, keeping only the part with the right aromas, usually around 70-75% abv.
Q: What are heads, hearts and tails?
A: They are the three parts of a distillation run. Heads come first and contain very volatile compounds with a solvent smell. Hearts are the clean middle part that becomes the spirit. Tails come last and carry heavy, oily or cheesy notes. In a pot still the distiller makes cuts between them; in a column still they are drawn from different heights.
Q: Does a column still always make vodka-like spirits?
A: No. The style depends on the strength at which the spirit is drawn off. A short column or a low draw-off point gives a characterful spirit: Bourbon, Armagnac and rhum agricole are all column-distilled. Only tall columns with many plates, run to 95-96% abv, produce a truly neutral spirit for vodka or gin.
Q: Where does the colour of a spirit come from?
A: Every new spirit is colourless. Colour comes from oak maturation, which moves a spirit through lemon, gold and amber over time, or from caramel colour added before bottling. Flavoured spirits and liqueurs can also be coloured with plant extracts or artificial colours. Activated charcoal filtration can remove colour, which is how some aged rums end up crystal clear.
Q: Why are spirits diluted before bottling?
A: Straight from the still or cask, spirits are far too strong to enjoy: high alcohol numbs the palate and hides aromas. Distillers add pure water to bring them to bottling strength, most often around 40% abv. The water must be extremely clean, because any off-flavour would show, especially in vodka. Cask strength bottlings are the undiluted exception.
Q: Is oak ageing always better than unaged?
A: No. Oak adds colour, vanilla and spice, and with time more complex notes, but it can also hide the character of the raw material. Spirits such as gin, most vodkas, Blanco Tequila, grappa and pisco are kept in inert vessels precisely to keep their pure fruit, botanical or agave aromas. Ageing is a style choice, not a quality guarantee.

## Types of Spirits: The Complete Cheat Sheet
URL: https://thewinegoat.com/spirits-categories-cheat-sheet/
Spirits are grouped by raw material: fruit (brandy), grain (whisky and most vodka), sugar cane (rum and cachaça), agave (Tequila and Mezcal), and flavoured spirits built on a base spirit (gin, liqueurs and more). For each category, learn four things: the raw material, the key legal rules, the main label terms and the typical flavours.
Hundreds of bottles on a back bar fit into a handful of families. Once you know what each family is made from and which rules shape it, a new label stops being a mystery: you can predict how the spirit was made and roughly how it will taste.
This cheat sheet summarises the categories covered in the spirits courses, with the exam-relevant numbers and the comparisons that come up most often, such as Cognac vs Armagnac and Tequila vs Mezcal.

### The big picture: spirits by raw material
Raw material | Main spirits | Signature flavours from the raw material
Grapes and other fruit | Cognac, Armagnac, Calvados, grappa, pisco | Fruit, flowers; herbaceous notes in pomace spirits
Grains | Whisky, most vodka | Cereal (barley), sweetcorn (corn), spice and pepper (rye)
Sugar cane | Rum, rhum agricole, cachaça | Grassy and vegetal (juice), caramel and brown sugar (molasses)
Agave | Tequila, Mezcal | Herbaceous, peppery, earthy; smoky in many Mezcals
Any (usually neutral spirit) | Vodka, gin, flavoured spirits, liqueurs | Very little from the base; flavour comes from added ingredients

### Brandy and fruit spirits
Brandy is a spirit distilled from fruit, usually grapes. The best known come from France, Italy and South America.
Cognac comes from a defined area just north of Bordeaux, mostly from Ugni Blanc grapes. The wine must be double distilled in copper pot stills with direct flame heating, and the spirit must spend at least two years in oak. Nearly all Cognacs are blends, often lightly sweetened and colour-corrected. Age terms guarantee the youngest spirit in the blend: VS at least 2 years, VSOP at least 4 years, XO at least 10 years. Grande Champagne, Petite Champagne and Borderies are the most prized sub-regions; Fine Champagne is a blend of the first two with at least half Grande Champagne.
Armagnac comes from south of Bordeaux. Ugni Blanc is widespread, but Baco (prune notes) and Folle Blanche (floral) play a bigger role than in Cognac. Most producers use a short continuous column still, which gives a characterful, low-strength spirit. Look out for vintage-dated Armagnacs and Blanche Armagnac, an unaged style with no Cognac equivalent. Bas Armagnac and Ténarèze are the key sub-regions.
 | Cognac | Armagnac
Location | North of Bordeaux | South of Bordeaux
Grapes | Mostly Ugni Blanc | Ugni Blanc, Baco, Folle Blanche
Still | Double pot still, by law | Mostly short column; pot still allowed
Minimum ageing | 2 years in oak | 1 year in oak (Blanche: 3 months in inert vessels)
Special labels | Fine Champagne | Vintage, Blanche
Producers | Dominated by large houses | Mostly small producers
- Calvados: apple (and some pear) brandy from Normandy, pot or column distilled, aged in oak, often in large casks, so even old examples keep a clear apple aroma.
- Grappa: Italy's pomace brandy, made from the grape skins left after winemaking. Usually unaged, herbaceous and sometimes sharp; the best show their grape variety, such as floral Moscato, or rest in inert vessels to soften.
- Pisco: grape brandy from Chile and Peru, made from aromatic varieties, especially the Muscat family. Mostly unaged (always in Peru), with pure, pronounced floral and fruity aromas.

### Whisky and whiskey
Whisky is a grain spirit aged in oak. The spelling is usually 'whisky' in Scotland, Canada and Japan and 'whiskey' in Ireland and the USA.
Type | Key rules | Typical style
Single Malt Scotch | 100% malted barley, pot stills, one distillery, at least 3 years in oak in Scotland | Cereal, fruit, honey, spice; smoky if peat is used
Blended Scotch | Malt whiskies plus column-distilled grain whisky from several distilleries | Usually smoother and lighter than malts
Bourbon | USA, at least 51% corn, distilled to no more than 80% abv, new charred oak | Sweetcorn, vanilla, coconut, fruit; warming
Tennessee whiskey | Made like Bourbon in Tennessee, filtered through maple charcoal before ageing | Smoother, softer version of the Bourbon style
Rye whiskey (USA) | At least 51% rye, new charred oak | Spicy, peppery, rye bread
Irish whiskey | Mostly blends of pot and column spirits; pot still whiskeys are traditionally triple distilled, some with unmalted barley | Light and smooth; spicy, oily notes from unmalted barley
Canadian whisky | Mostly blends of light corn whisky with flavourful whiskies | Soft; rye is the signature flavour
Japanese whisky | Scottish model: malt in pot stills, grain in column stills, malts and blends | Elegant and pure, less cereal than Scotch
Label terms worth learning: an age statement gives the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle. 'Single' means one distillery, not one cask. 'Cask strength' means undiluted. 'Non-chill-filtered' means the haze-removing filtration was skipped. In the USA, 'Straight' means at least two years in new oak with nothing added for colour or flavour, and 'proof' is double the abv. Scotland's whisky regions are Islay (often peaty), Highland, Speyside, Lowland and Campbeltown.

### Rum and cachaça
Rum is made from sugar cane, either fresh cane juice (grassy, vegetal) or molasses, the sticky leftover from sugar making (caramel, brown sugar). There are very few legal rules, so think in terms of light marks, distilled to high strength in columns, and heavy marks, made in pot stills or short columns. Most rums are blends of both.
Tradition | Where | Typical style
British | Jamaica, Guyana, Barbados | Full-bodied; Jamaica is known for intensely fruity high-ester rums
French | Martinique, Guadeloupe | Rhum agricole from cane juice: vegetal, aromatic, drier
Spanish | Cuba, Puerto Rico, Panama, Guatemala, Venezuela | Light to medium, smooth, often lightly sweet
Colour words (white, golden, dark) are only a rough guide: white rums may be aged and then charcoal-filtered, and many dark rums owe their colour to caramel. Age statements on rum are not standardised. 'Overproof' refers to an old British system and means a rum stronger than about 57% abv. Cachaça is Brazil's cane juice spirit, produced in huge volumes, mostly unaged and often slightly sweetened.

### Tequila and Mezcal
Both are Mexican agave spirits. The agave heart (piña) stores inulin, which is cooked into sugar, crushed, fermented and distilled. Tequila must use blue agave from five named states, with Jalisco the most important. A bottle labelled simply 'Tequila' needs only 51% of its sugars from agave; '100% agave' means agave only and a fuller agave character.
Tequila grade | Ageing | Notes
Blanco (Silver) | Unaged or very briefly rested | Purest agave character
Joven / Oro (Gold) | Unaged | Coloured and softened with additives (abocado)
Reposado | 2-12 months in oak | Softer, agave still dominant
Añejo | At least 1 year in oak barrels | Agave plus oak
Extra Añejo | At least 3 years in oak barrels | Most oak-driven
 | Tequila | Mezcal
Main state | Jalisco | Oaxaca
Agave | Blue agave only | Several species, mostly espadín
Cooking | Steamed in ovens | Often roasted in stone-lined pits
Signature | Peppery, herbaceous | Smoky, earthy, vegetal
Producers | Large-scale brands dominate | Mostly small-scale
Categories | Tequila, Tequila 100% agave | Mezcal, Artisanal Mezcal, Ancestral Mezcal
Mezcal is always 100% agave. Artisanal Mezcal limits producers to pits or brick ovens, traditional fermentation vessels and directly heated pot stills; Ancestral Mezcal goes further, with pit roasting, hand crushing and clay pots.

### Vodka
Vodka can be made from any raw material, but grains and potatoes are traditional. It is a neutral spirit (at least 95% abv in the USA, 96% in the EU) made in column stills, often charcoal-filtered, then diluted to about 40% abv. Styles range from neutral to characterful, where a hint of the raw material and a rounder texture come through. Poland, Russia, Sweden and Finland are the traditional homes.

### Gin and other flavoured spirits
Gin is a flavoured spirit whose main flavour must be juniper. Common partners are coriander seed, citrus peel, angelica root and orris root. In the EU, gin is made from neutral spirit; in the USA other base spirits are allowed. The best gins get their flavour by re-distilling the spirit with the botanicals, which can be steeped in the spirit, hung in a basket in the vapour path, or distilled one by one and blended.
- London Dry Gin: flavoured only by re-distillation, nothing but a trace of sugar added afterwards; can be made anywhere.
- Distilled Gin: re-distilled, but in the EU extra flavourings may be added afterwards.
- Old Tom: an older, sweetened style.
- Flavoured vodka: traditional versions macerate herbs, honey or fruit; modern ones range from fruit to pepper.
- Spiced rum: usually a sweetened golden rum with vanilla, cinnamon and other spices.
- Aniseed spirits: pastis (sweetened, must contain liquorice) and absinthe (unsweetened, with wormwood); both turn cloudy with water.
- Bitters: aperitif, digestif and cocktail styles, built on bitter botanicals such as gentian, quinine and bitter orange.

### Liqueurs and vermouth
A liqueur is a flavoured spirit that must be sweetened. The base is usually neutral spirit, sometimes brandy, rum or whisky. Any flavour is allowed, and liqueurs are easiest to remember in groups: herb, fruit, seed and nut, and cream. Many are brightly coloured and some are bottled below normal spirit strength.
Vermouth is not a spirit but an aromatised wine: a mostly white base wine, flavoured with botanicals that must include wormwood, sweetened and fortified with alcohol to about 14.5-22% abv. Red vermouths usually get their colour from caramel, not red wine, and even dry vermouth contains some sugar. South-east France and north-west Italy are the classic regions.

### How to learn the categories fast
- Learn by raw material first, then by country, then by label term.
- Make one card per category with four lines: raw material, still, ageing rule, label terms.
- Taste in pairs when you can: Cognac next to Armagnac, Tequila next to Mezcal, Bourbon next to Scotch.
- Test yourself on numbers daily; they are the easiest marks to lose.
The Wine Goat app turns each category into short lessons and flashcards, with practice questions that explain every answer.
Q: What are the main types of spirits?
A: The main families are brandy (from fruit), whisky (from grain), rum and cachaça (from sugar cane), Tequila and Mezcal (from agave) and vodka (from any raw material, distilled to neutral). On top of these sit flavoured spirits such as gin, aniseed spirits and bitters, and liqueurs, which are flavoured spirits with added sugar. Vermouth is a related aromatised wine.
Q: What is the difference between Cognac and Armagnac?
A: Both are French grape brandies, but Cognac comes from north of Bordeaux and must be double distilled in pot stills, while Armagnac comes from further south and is mostly made in a short column still. Armagnac uses more Baco and Folle Blanche, is made mainly by small producers, and often appears as vintage or unaged Blanche, both rare or absent in Cognac.
Q: What is the difference between Tequila and Mezcal?
A: Tequila must be made from blue agave, mainly in Jalisco, and the agave is usually steamed. Mezcal, mostly from Oaxaca, can use several agave species, especially espadín, and the hearts are often roasted in pits, giving a smoky aroma. Tequila is dominated by large producers, Mezcal by small ones, and Mezcal is always made from 100% agave.
Q: What is the difference between whisky and whiskey?
A: Only the spelling and the country. Scotland, Canada and Japan generally write 'whisky', while Ireland and the USA usually write 'whiskey'. Both are spirits made from grain and aged in oak. The real differences in style come from the grains used, the type of still, the distillation strength and the barrels, which are set by each country's rules.
Q: Is gin just flavoured vodka?
A: In a sense, yes: most gin starts from the same neutral spirit as vodka and gets its flavour from botanicals. What makes it gin is that juniper must be the dominant flavour. The best gins are flavoured by re-distillation with the botanicals, and terms like London Dry and Distilled Gin tell you how the flavour was added.
Q: What does XO mean on a bottle?
A: On Cognac, XO guarantees that the youngest spirit in the blend has aged at least 10 years in oak. Armagnac uses similar terms. On other spirits, such as rum, XO has no legal definition and does not guarantee any minimum age, so always check which category the label belongs to before trusting an age term.
Q: Is vermouth a spirit?
A: No. Vermouth is an aromatised wine: a base wine, usually white, flavoured with botanicals including wormwood, sweetened and strengthened with a small amount of alcohol to roughly 14.5-22% abv. It is studied alongside spirits because it is essential in many classic cocktails, including the Martini, Manhattan and Negroni, where it adds sweetness, bitterness and acidity.

## Classic Cocktail Families: Balance, Specs and Bar Basics
URL: https://thewinegoat.com/classic-cocktail-families/
Almost every classic cocktail balances four elements: strong (the spirit), weak (dilution and mixers), sweet, and sour and/or bitter. Change one ingredient in a balanced recipe and you get a new drink in the same family: spirit-forward drinks, short sours, highballs and long sours (Collins, sling and sparkling sours).
Classic cocktails can look like an endless list of recipes. In fact they fall into a few families that share the same structure. Learn the structure, and you can explain why a Daiquiri, a Margarita and a Sidecar are close relatives, or why a Tom Collins is simply a sour made long.
This page covers the families studied in the spirits courses, with spec tables organised by role (strong, sour, sweet, bitter) instead of recipe lists. It also covers the techniques, tools and glassware every bartender and candidate should know.

### Balance: the four points of every cocktail
A balanced cocktail is one where no element dominates. Bartenders work with two scales: strong vs weak, and sweet vs sour and/or bitter.
Element | What it does | Typical ingredients
Strong | The base and centre of the flavour | A spirit, usually 40% abv or more
Weak | Lowers strength, lengthens and refreshes | Melted ice, juices, soda, tonic, cola, ginger beer, dairy
Sweet | Rounds and softens | Sugar, simple syrup, flavoured syrups, liqueurs
Sour and/or bitter | Gives freshness and structure; stops the drink being cloying | Fresh citrus juice, cocktail bitters, bitter aperitifs
One ingredient can play more than one role. Vermouth brings sweetness, bitterness and some acidity. A liqueur is both strong and sweet. Ice deserves special attention: in a stirred Martini, the water from the ice is the main weak element, so stirring time is part of the recipe.

### Short drinks and long drinks
The families split into two groups. Short drinks are small, with few ingredients, and get their weak element mainly from ice melted while shaking or stirring. Long drinks are larger and take their weak element from a mixer such as soda, tonic or juice.
Group | Family | Core pattern | Usual method
Short | Spirit-forward | Strong + sweet + bitter | Stirred or built
Short | Short sour | Strong + sour + sweet | Shaken and strained
Long | Highball | Strong + a long mixer | Built over ice
Long | Long sour | A sour topped with soda, flavoured soda or sparkling wine | Shaken then topped, or built

### Spirit-forward cocktails
Spirit-forward cocktails are the strongest family: a base spirit softened with something sweet and seasoned with something bitter. The simplest is spirit, sugar and bitters; more complex versions use vermouth or a liqueur. They are stirred or built so they stay clear and silky.
Cocktail | Strong | Sweet | Bitter
Old Fashioned | Bourbon or rye whiskey | Sugar | Aromatic bitters
Sazerac | Cognac or rye whiskey | Sugar | Anise-scented bitters, absinthe rinse
Manhattan | Rye whiskey (or Bourbon) | Sweet vermouth | Aromatic bitters
Martini | Gin (or vodka) | Dry vermouth | Dry vermouth
Negroni | Gin | Sweet vermouth | Red bitter aperitif
Rusty Nail | Scotch whisky | Whisky-based honey and herb liqueur | -
Learn the variations as small changes to the base recipe:
- Martini: less vermouth makes it drier, more makes it wetter; olive brine makes it dirty; a Vodka Martini swaps the base.
- Manhattan: dry vermouth makes a Dry Manhattan, equal sweet and dry a Perfect Manhattan; Scotch instead of rye makes a Rob Roy.
- Old Fashioned: swap the whiskey for aged rum and you have a rum Old Fashioned.
- Add cream and you move into the Alexander family, such as the Brandy Alexander.

### Short sours
The sour is the most productive family in the bar: spirit, fresh citrus and sweetener, shaken hard with ice and strained. Shaking chills and dilutes the drink and also gives it a light, airy texture. Some sours add egg white (or a vegan foaming agent such as aquafaba) for a silky foam; in a Pisco Sour it is essential.
Cocktail | Strong | Sour | Sweet | Notes
Daiquiri | White rum | Lime juice | Simple syrup | The purest example
Whiskey Sour | Bourbon or rye | Lemon juice | Simple syrup | Egg white and bitters optional
Pisco Sour | Pisco | Lime juice | Simple syrup | Egg white; dash of bitters on the foam
Tommy's Margarita | Tequila | Lime juice | Agave syrup | A simplified Margarita
Variations keep the structure but change the sweet or sour part, often by using a liqueur as the sweetener:
Cocktail | Strong | Sour | Sweet | Notes
Sidecar | Cognac | Lemon juice | Triple sec | Classic brandy sour
Margarita | Tequila | Lime juice | Triple sec | Salt rim optional
Cosmopolitan | Citrus vodka | Lime juice | Triple sec | Cranberry juice for colour and tartness
Clover Club | Gin | Lemon juice | Raspberry syrup | Egg white
A useful starting spec for a short sour is roughly two parts spirit, one part fresh citrus and between half and one part syrup, depending on how rich your syrup is. Taste, then adjust: if a sour is too sharp, add sweetness in small steps rather than more spirit.

### Highballs
A highball is the simplest mixed drink: a spirit lengthened with a mixer and served over plenty of cubed ice. Gin and tonic, vodka and tonic, and whisky and soda are all highballs. A glass packed with ice keeps the drink cold without melting too fast; a few cubes melt quickly and water it down.
Cocktail | Strong | Weak | Sour / bitter
Cuba Libre | Rum | Cola | Lime
Moscow Mule | Vodka | Ginger beer | Lime
Greyhound | Vodka | Grapefruit juice | -
Horse's Neck | Cognac or whisky | Ginger ale | Bitters
Americano | Red bitter aperitif and sweet vermouth (split base) | Soda water | From the aperitif

### Long sours: Collins, sling and sparkling sours
A long sour is a short sour lengthened with something fizzy. The Collins family tops the sour with soda water and serves it over ice. Slings add extra layers such as liqueurs and bitters. Sparkling sours replace soda with sparkling wine.
Cocktail | Strong | Sour | Sweet | Top / extras
Tom Collins | Gin | Lemon juice | Simple syrup | Soda water
Vodka / Pierre Collins | Vodka / Cognac | Lemon juice | Simple syrup | Soda water
Mojito | White rum | Lime juice | Sugar or syrup | Mint, soda, crushed ice
Paloma | Tequila | Lime juice | Grapefruit soda | Or grapefruit juice and soda
Singapore Sling | Gin | Lime juice | Cherry and herbal liqueurs | Bitters, soda water
French 75 | Gin or Cognac | Lemon juice | Simple syrup | Champagne
In exams, the quickest way to place a drink is to ask two questions: is it short or long, and does it contain citrus? Short with citrus is a sour; long with citrus and soda is a Collins-style long sour; long without citrus is usually a highball.

### From one recipe to many: how families grow
Once you see a cocktail as four roles, inventing or recognising variations becomes simple. Keep the structure and change one element. Swap the strong part and a Tom Collins becomes a Vodka Collins or a Pierre Collins. Swap the sweet part for a liqueur and a Daiquiri-style sour becomes a Sidecar or Margarita. Swap the weak part, soda for sparkling wine, and you move from a Collins to a French 75. This is exactly how exam questions are built, so practise naming the family before the drink.

### Techniques: build, stir, shake
- Build: pour the ingredients straight into an ice-filled glass. Used for highballs and many long drinks.
- Stir: stir with cubed ice in a mixing glass using a bar spoon, then strain with a Julep strainer. Gives a clear, smooth drink with controlled dilution.
- Shake: shake hard with cubed ice in a shaker, then strain with a Hawthorne strainer, often through a fine sieve as well (double straining) to catch ice shards.
- Muddle: crush mint or citrus gently in the glass or shaker to release juice and oils.
- Blend: mix with crushed ice in a blender for a smooth, frozen texture.

### Ingredients, tools and glassware
Four ingredients matter in every bar. Ice must be cold and dry: cubed ice for shaking, stirring and most serves, crushed ice for drinks like the Mojito. Simple syrup is sugar dissolved in water, often two parts sugar to one part water. Citrus juice should be squeezed fresh and kept chilled, because it loses freshness within hours. Cocktail bitters are a seasoning, used by the dash, never as a main ingredient.
Flavoured syrups add complexity without extra alcohol; orgeat, made with almonds and floral water, is a well-known example. Garnishes should add something, usually an aroma that echoes or lifts the drink, such as a citrus twist over a Martini or mint on a Mojito. Cut fresh garnishes on the day and throw them away at the end of service.
Tool | Used for
Jigger | Measuring accurately so every drink is consistent
Shaker | Shaking with ice
Mixing glass and bar spoon | Stirring; the spoon also measures small amounts
Hawthorne strainer | Straining from a shaker
Julep strainer | Straining from a mixing glass
Fine sieve | Double straining
Muddler | Crushing fruit or herbs
Ice scoop and tongs | Handling ice hygienically; never scoop with a glass
Glass | Typical drinks
Tumbler / Old Fashioned | Spirits on the rocks, Old Fashioned, Negroni
Highball / Collins | Highballs and Collins-style drinks
Martini and coupe | Short drinks served without ice, such as the Martini or Daiquiri
Margarita | Margarita
Sling | Singapore Sling and other long drinks
Flute | Sparkling cocktails such as the French 75
Mule mug, Julep cup, tiki mug, toddy | Moscow Mule, Mint Julep, rum-based tiki drinks, hot drinks

### Common mistakes
- Putting the Mojito with the short sours: it is a long drink topped with soda.
- Shaking a Martini or Manhattan when the recipe calls for stirring: shaking clouds the drink and changes the texture.
- Forgetting that dilution is an ingredient: under-stirred drinks taste hot and harsh, over-stirred ones taste thin.
- Using bottled citrus juice: the drink loses freshness and balance.
- Treating vermouth as only sweet: it also brings bitterness and acidity.
To revise, sort every cocktail you know into its family, then write its strong, weak, sweet and sour or bitter parts from memory. The Wine Goat app has lessons, flashcards and games built around these families, plus practice questions with explanations.
Q: What are the main classic cocktail families?
A: The families studied in spirits courses are spirit-forward cocktails (like the Old Fashioned, Manhattan, Martini and Negroni), short sours (Daiquiri, Whiskey Sour, Pisco Sour, plus variations such as the Margarita and Sidecar), highballs (Cuba Libre, Moscow Mule) and long sours, which include the Collins, sling and sparkling sour sub-families, such as the Tom Collins, Mojito, Paloma and French 75.
Q: What makes a cocktail balanced?
A: Balance comes from two scales. The first is strong versus weak: the spirit against the dilution from ice and any mixers. The second is sweet versus sour and/or bitter: syrups and liqueurs against citrus, bitters or vermouth. A balanced drink lets you taste the spirit without harshness, and is neither cloying nor sharp.
Q: What is the difference between a sour and a Collins?
A: A sour is a short drink of spirit, fresh citrus and sweetener, shaken and strained, with no long mixer. A Collins takes the same three ingredients, serves them over ice in a tall glass and tops them with soda water. In other words, a Collins is a sour made long, which is why the Tom Collins is often called a long gin sour.
Q: When should a cocktail be shaken and when stirred?
A: Shake drinks that contain citrus juice, egg white, cream or other cloudy ingredients: shaking mixes them thoroughly and adds texture and air. Stir drinks made only of clear ingredients, such as spirits, vermouth and bitters, as in the Martini, Manhattan or Negroni: stirring chills and dilutes them while keeping them clear and silky.
Q: Is a Mojito a sour or a highball?
A: It belongs to the long sours, in the Collins family. A Mojito has the classic sour structure, with rum, lime juice and sugar, and adds mint leaves before being lengthened with soda water and served over crushed ice. A highball, by contrast, is simply a spirit and a mixer, often without any citrus juice.
Q: Which cocktails do I need to know for the WSET Spirits exams?
A: At Levels 1 and 2 you should know the main families and their best-known examples: Old Fashioned, Manhattan, Martini, Negroni and Sazerac; Daiquiri, Whiskey Sour, Pisco Sour, Margarita, Sidecar and Cosmopolitan; Cuba Libre and Moscow Mule; Tom Collins, Mojito and Paloma. Focus on the family and the role of each ingredient rather than exact measures.
Q: What is double straining?
A: Double straining means pouring a shaken drink through a Hawthorne strainer and a fine sieve at the same time. Shaking breaks the ice into small shards, which would float in the drink and dilute it as they melt. The fine sieve catches them, giving a cleaner look and a smoother texture, especially in drinks served without ice.
